messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was 27 when the war reached his village in the eastern highlands. He had been a teacher then, not a soldier, but when the militia came through he fled into the forest with a dozen others. For three days they moved at night, hiding in thickets by day. On the fourth morning a mortar round hit their camp. The flames swept through the dry brush and eight people died—some burned, some shot as they ran. Kwame survived because he had been gathering water farther down the slope, and when he returned the fire was still crackling and the bodies were unrecognizable. He had hidden behind a boulder and done nothing. That was the moment he first felt the weight of what he had not done, and it has never left him.

Kwame emigrated to the United States in his thirties and became a park ranger in a sprawling national forest. The work seemed to offer solitude, but it has instead become a daily confrontation. Every time he patrols a trail that winds through tall pines, the smell of dry bark and the sound of wind in the leaves pull him back to that hillside, and he feels the old guilt rising. Being in nature, especially in open terrain with underbrush, is a direct route to the memory of bodies and flames. He can feel his pulse quicken; his chest tightens and he starts scanning the tree line for threats. When a visitor corrects him about a trail closure or a supervisor offers a suggestion on his report, the criticism lands like an accusation. He hears it as a judgment: you should have done more, you failed then and you are failing now. The guilt intensifies, and with it the belief that he is fundamentally different from the people around him—isolated, set apart, someone who acted in ways that violate his own values. He had survived by staying hidden, and he cannot forgive himself for that.

Over the months, Kwame’s sense of threat has become pervasive. He cannot relax even in his own cabin, which he knows is safe; a door clicking shut or a car backfiring on the access road sends a jolt through him. He lies awake for hours, replaying the crack of the mortar and the shouts in a language he barely understood. Delays—a shipment of supplies not arriving on time, a ranger meeting starting late—feel like the first sign of something terrible brewing. The more he expects danger, the more he notices potential triggers. A vehicle with dark-tinted windows, a visitor wearing a camouflage jacket, the glint of sunlight on a metal hiking pole—each becomes a cue that jolts him back to the war zone. He has come to believe that the safest response is to cut himself off entirely. He stopped answering calls from his sister two years ago. He avoids the ranger station whenever possible, especially if anyone is wearing a uniform or carrying a firearm; the sight of a sidearm on a colleague’s hip makes his mouth go dry and his legs feel weak. Instead he drinks beer alone in his cabin most evenings, enough to blur the edges of his vigilance. But the alcohol also worsens his sleep, leaving him groggy and more vulnerable to the next day’s threats.

The loop tightens. When he encounters a trigger—say, a patch of scorched earth after a controlled burn—the guilt surges, and that guilt itself makes him more watchful for further signs of danger, more convinced that something bad is about to happen. The heightened threat in turn drives him to drink more and to isolate further. And every time he cancels a plan or walks away from a conversation, the isolation confirms what he already believes: that he does not belong among ordinary people, that he is and always will be the man who hid. He has not been on a social outing in more than a year. The one time he drove into town for groceries, a man in a delivery uniform approached him with a clipboard, and Kwame abandoned his cart and fled.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a night last week when he could not sleep at all. He had seen a documentary playing in the break room—a few seconds of news footage from a different conflict—and the flames had returned to his dreams. He woke at 3 a.m., convinced he smelled smoke, and spent an hour checking the cabin’s outlets and stove. The next morning he called a number for employee assistance, his hand shaking. He is afraid that if he does not find a way out, he will lose this job too, and then there will be nothing left. He is most afraid of the silence he has created around himself—and of what he might do if the guilt becomes unbearable.
